title: Renewable Energy
summary: Explore renewable energy for Africa: why it matters, solar PV and solar thermal, wind power and the cube law, hydropower and geothermal, bioenergy and clean cooking, and storage, grids and careers. All calculations were checked in code.
audience: Students, technicians, entrepreneurs, policymakers and anyone interested in clean energy

body.p: Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replenished: sunlight, wind, flowing water, the Earth's heat and biomass. It reduces greenhouse emissions and air pollution, and because sunshine and wind are free, it protects countries from volatile fuel prices.

list: Hundreds of millions of people in sub-Saharan Africa still lack electricity, and many more rely on unreliable grids or diesel generators.
Africa has some of the world's best solar resources, strong winds in the north, east and south, large hydropower potential and geothermal energy in the East African Rift.
Off-grid solar home systems and mini-grids can bring power to rural areas faster and more cheaply than extending the grid.
Renewables create local jobs in installation, maintenance, manufacturing and finance.

body.p: Challenges include high upfront costs, access to finance, weak grids that struggle with variable output, and the need for skilled technicians and good policy.

body.tip: Compare energy options by the cost per kWh over the full life of the system, not just the purchase price.

body.p: Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels turn light directly into electricity; solar thermal systems use sunlight to heat water or air.

list: Solar PV ranges from small lanterns and home systems to rooftop systems and utility-scale plants with millions of panels.

Solar water heaters (geysers) can supply most of a household's hot water. Heating 250 litres a day of water by 45 °C needs about 250 x 4200 x 45 J, which is 47.25 million J or roughly 13.1 kWh a day, if done with electricity, so solar heating saves a lot.
Concentrated solar power (CSP) uses mirrors to focus sunlight and drive turbines; plants operate in Morocco and South Africa, often with heat storage for the evening.
Solar pumps for irrigation and drinking water replace diesel pumps in many rural areas.

body.p: A plant does not run at full power all the time. The capacity factor is actual output divided by maximum possible output. A 100 MW solar plant with a 20% capacity factor produces about 100 x 8760 x 0.2 = 175 200 MWh a year (there are 8760 hours in a year).

body.tip: Our separate Solar PV Basics course covers sizing and installing solar home systems in detail.

body.p: Wind turbines turn the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity. The power in the wind is P = ½ρAv³, where ρ is air density (about 1.225 kg/m³), A is the swept area of the blades and v is wind speed.

Blades 20 m long sweep an area of π x 20² = about 1256.6 m². At 8 m/s, the wind power is 0.5 x 1.225 x 1256.6 x 8³, about 394 kW. Turbines capture only part of this; with a power coefficient of 0.4, the output is about 158 kW. The theoretical maximum, the Betz limit, is about 59%.

list: Because power depends on v³, doubling wind speed gives 2³ = 8 times the power. Site selection is critical.
Taller towers reach stronger, steadier winds.
Large wind farms operate in Kenya (Lake Turkana), South Africa, Morocco, Egypt and Ethiopia.
Capacity factors for good wind sites are often 30 to 45%: a 100 MW wind farm at 35% gives about 306 600 MWh a year.

body.tip: Measure wind at a site for at least a year before investing; small differences in average speed make big differences in output.

body.p: Hydropower uses falling or flowing water to turn turbines. Power is P = ρgQHη, where Q is flow in m³/s, H is the head (height of fall) and η is efficiency. A flow of 2 m³/s falling 50 m at 85% efficiency gives 1000 x 9.81 x 2 x 50 x 0.85, about 834 kW.

list: Large dams such as Kariba, Cahora Bassa, Inga and the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam supply much of the power in their regions.
Small and micro-hydro schemes can power villages and farms from streams.
Benefits: reliable, flexible output and long life. Concerns: displacement of communities, effects on rivers and fish, and vulnerability to droughts.

body.p: Geothermal plants use heat from deep underground to produce steam that drives turbines. Kenya is a world leader, with large plants at Olkaria in the Rift Valley supplying a major share of its electricity. Ethiopia, Tanzania and other Rift countries are developing resources too. Geothermal provides steady baseload power, day and night.

body.tip: Hydro output depends on rainfall; spreading investment across different sources makes a power system more resilient.

body.p: Bioenergy comes from organic material: wood, crop residues, manure and organic waste. Traditional use of firewood and charcoal is the main cooking fuel for many African households, contributing to deforestation and harmful indoor smoke.

list: Biogas digesters let bacteria break down manure and food waste without oxygen to make methane-rich gas for cooking and lighting. The leftover slurry is a good fertiliser. Household digesters fed by a few cows can supply much of a family's cooking gas.
Improved cookstoves burn wood or charcoal more efficiently, cutting fuel use and smoke.
LPG, ethanol and electric cooking (including efficient electric pressure cookers) are cleaner options where available.
Biofuels such as bioethanol from sugarcane can replace some petrol, but must not compete with food crops or cause forest clearing.

body.p: Sustainable bioenergy depends on replanting and using waste rather than clearing forests.

body.tip: A biogas digester needs regular feeding and the right mix of water and manure; training users is as important as building it.

body.p: Solar and wind vary with weather and time of day, so power systems need flexibility.

list: Batteries, mostly lithium-ion, store energy for hours and support mini-grids and home systems. A 5 kWh battery used to 80% supplies 4 kWh.
Pumped hydro storage pumps water uphill when power is cheap and releases it through turbines at peak times.
Mixing sources (solar by day, wind often stronger at night, hydro as a flexible backup) smooths supply.
Regional power pools, such as the Southern African Power Pool, let countries trade electricity.
Smart meters and demand management shift use to times when power is plentiful.

body.p: The sector needs installers, electricians, engineers, project developers, financial analysts, policy experts and sales and after-sales staff. Supportive policies, such as auction programmes for independent power producers, clear rules for mini-grids and net metering for rooftop solar, attract investment.

body.tip: Learn both technical skills and customer service; many solar businesses succeed or fail on after-sales support.
